name: Mongol Empire steppe warfare

weightNotes.aggression: Strategically relentless offensives (Khwarazm 1219-21, Rus 1237-40, Hungary and Poland 1241, Baghdad 1258), but tactically they declined fights on bad terms, so not 1.0.
weightNotes.maneuver: Pure manoeuvre: every man mounted with three or four horses, multiple columns, deep raids and envelopment (May, Mongol Art of War).
weightNotes.flanking: Encirclement was the standard battle plan; at Legnica (1241) feigned attacks and withdrawals by dispersed groups drew the enemy away from its main body into ambush.
weightNotes.siegePreference: They destroyed the field army first, then took cities systematically with captured and hired engineers (Xiangyang 1273, counterweight trebuchets built by Persian and Syrian engineers). Field battle first, siege second.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Commanders held back heavy cavalry to receive an enemy drawn on by the feigned retreat (Kalka 1223, Mohi 1241); moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Screens of scouts far ahead and pre-war intelligence: Subutai sent spies into Poland, Hungary and eastern Austria before 1241. Best in era.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Mongol units broke contact early rather than accept attritional losses, then returned; the feigned retreat is the extreme form. Low threshold = early disengagement, not fragility.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Light horse archers, heavy lancers, conscripted infantry and Chinese and Persian siege engineers with gunpowder weapons (Khwarazm campaign order of battle). Infantry weak, so not higher.
weightNotes.initiative: Decimal units (tumen of 10,000) under commanders who operated independently for years across continents (Jebe and Subutai 1220-23), coordinated by the yam relay. High.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Armies moved with their herds and remounts and lived off pasture and plunder, so they ranged far beyond any supply network (low strictness), yet campaigns were timed to grass and halted when pasture failed. 0.45.

summary: A fully mounted army organised in decimal units (10, 100, 1,000, 10,000) with three or four horses per man. Columns advanced on a broad front, separated by days but converging on a target, after long intelligence preparation. In battle, light horse archers wore down and disordered the enemy with arrows and feigned withdrawals, drawing pursuers into envelopment and a final charge by heavy lancers. Fortified cities were taken by conscripted labour and Chinese and Persian engineers with trebuchets and gunpowder weapons, and resistance was punished by massacre to induce surrender elsewhere.
whyItWorked: Mobility and remounts gave them the choice of where and when to fight; superior scouting and intelligence meant they usually knew more than the enemy; discipline and decimal organisation let dispersed columns coordinate over hundreds of kilometres; adopting foreign siege engineering removed the classic nomad weakness against walls.
whereItFailed: Against an enemy who used their own methods with better local knowledge and numbers: Ain Jalut (1260), where Baibars's feigned retreat drew Kitbuqa's reduced force into an ambush in the hills. Where horses and pasture could not follow: the invasions of Japan (1274, 1281) were wrecked at sea by typhoons and stopped on the beaches; Syria and Vietnam campaigns were limited by grazing and climate. Succession politics also halted campaigns (withdrawal from Hungary 1242).
